## The current release. Use this one.

Guardrails for desktop AI agents, in Swift. Secret redaction and SSRF policy for anything
that reads your screen and follows links. Zero external packages, MIT.

```swift
// Package.swift
.package(url: "https://github.com/dotcomjack/grux.git", from: "0.6.1")
.product(name: "Grux", package: "grux")
// then, in your source
import Grux
```

Your own manifest needs `platforms: [.macOS(.v14)]` too. That line is not optional and
leaving it out is a build failure, not a warning. The
[README](https://github.com/dotcomjack/grux#platforms-and-the-whole-manifest) carries the
whole manifest, pragma and import included, and a test in the suite fails the build if any
Swift block in the README is missing either.

115 tests, 0 failures, on macOS 14 and macOS 15.

## The minimum platform is now macOS 14, up from 13

This is a real break for anyone on macOS 13 and it is not cosmetic tidying.

`testEveryUnicodeSpellingOfALoopbackHostIsDenied` defends against a homograph loopback
SSRF, and it holds because Foundation's `URL.host` applies UTS46 mapping. macOS 15 ships
the rewritten swift-foundation URL parser, while 13 and 14 ship the older one, so the
declared minimum needed its own CI leg. The `macos-13` runner never scheduled: 31 minutes
queued while 14 and 15 finished in about two, and it held the whole run in `queued` so CI
could never conclude at all. GitHub is retiring that runner.

Rather than keep advertising a floor no CI leg can ever prove, the floor moved to the
lowest version that is proven. macOS 14 passing is the evidence that matters here, because
14 ships the same older parser the concern was about.

## Two provider patterns added

Docker Hub `dckr_pat_` and Linear `lin_api_`. Both were invisible to every pass: they are
single case, or carry no digit, so no entropy rule reaches them without eating ordinary
text. They are distinctive prefixes that appear in no ordinary prose, so adding them widens
what is caught without widening what is destroyed. That is the entire reason these two
shipped and the two leaks below did not.

## RFC 2765 IPv4-translated IPv6 is now decoded

`::ffff:0:127.0.0.1` was the fourth member of the embedded-IPv4 family and the only one
`URLGuard` did not judge by the address it carries. It is not routable on macOS today, so
this is hardening rather than a live bypass, but the guard already denies `0x7f.0.0.1` on
the chance a resolver reads it as loopback, and already denies deprecated site-local
`fec0::/10`.

**The first attempt at that fix was wrong in a way worth recording.** It pinned the `ffff`
group to one byte position, which catches `::ffff:0:a.b.c.d` and misses
`::ffff:0:0:a.b.c.d`, because how many explicit zero groups the author writes moves the
group from index 5 to 4 to 3. The check now judges the family by SHAPE, the leading twelve
bytes being all zero except at most one aligned `ffff` group, which covers every spelling.

## Disclosed, not fixed

Two findings from the same audit round are disclosed in the README's limits section rather
than fixed, and the reason is a measurement rather than a shrug.

- **A labelled credential inside a JSON array or a YAML sequence survives.**
  `{"passwords": ["s3cretPassw0rdForProd"]}` comes back untouched while
  `POSTGRES_PASSWORD=` with the identical secret is caught.
- **An XML or plist element BODY survives**, though the attribute form is caught.
  `<password>value</password>` goes through. Maven `settings.xml` and Apple `.plist` files
  both put credentials in element bodies.

Both are the same adjacency problem: the credential-word rules read a name and the value
next to it, and a bracket or a tag between them breaks that. Widening those rules is the
one change measured to make things WORSE, because they already destroy 20 of 30 ordinary
config lines whose field name merely contains a credential word, including `"author"` in
every `package.json` and the OIDC `auth_url` and `token_url`. Both are pinned by
`testKnownDefect*` tests written as the assertion that should hold wrapped in
`XCTExpectFailure`, so fixing either turns the suite red and forces the fixer to delete the
expectation deliberately.

## The six tags before 0.5.0 leak credentials, and they stay resolvable

0.1.0, 0.2.0, 0.2.1, 0.3.0, 0.3.1 and 0.4.0 all leak, each one was found by an audit of
code that had already survived earlier rounds, and every one of them looked fine when it
was cut. Each has its own release here saying what it does.

They are not deleted and the history is not rewritten. Deleting a tag buys nothing against
an attacker, since clones, forks and cached commit views survive it, it breaks anyone
pinned to an old tag, and it destroys the disclosure record that is the reason to trust
this release.

**Be precise about whose credentials leaked.** The library failed to redact ITS USERS'
secrets: a credential a caller passed into `SecretRedactor.redact` could survive the
redactor and reach the model. No credential belonging to the author has ever been in this
repository, and every credential-shaped string under `Tests/` is synthetic.
